narrative:
The model predicted an 80% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and this probability is well above their threshold, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades had the strongest influence. Placing in the second decile is noticeably weaker than the average of nearly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted, and this pulled the prediction strongly toward failure. Your family income bracket came next; being from an upper-middle income background pushed the outcome slightly further toward failure compared with the mix of backgrounds among admitted students. Your LSAT score was the third most important factor and worked in the opposite direction. At 35 it sits a little below the 37.2 average of accepted students, yet it still provided a modest pull toward passing.

Taken together, the negative effect of your third-year academic standing outweighed the modest positive signal from your LSAT, resulting in the high predicted risk of failure.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record, particularly by improving performance in later-year courses, and consider retaking the LSAT to raise that score. These steps would most directly address the factors that led to the rejection. (218 words)
